title: Socles and the Onan Scott Landscape

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups and the socle of a finite group
Distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize one another
items.strategy: For minimal normal subgroups M and N, the commutator subgroup [M,N] is normal in both and lies in M intersect N. Minimality forces [M,N] to be trivial unless M=N, so distinct minimal normal subgroups commute.

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups of finite groups are characteristically simple
items.strategy: If M is minimal normal in G and K is a characteristic subgroup of M, then K is normal in G. Minimality of M forces K to be trivial or all of M, so M has no proper nontrivial characteristic subgroup.

items.title: Finite characteristically simple groups are direct products of isomorphic simple groups
items.strategy: Choose a minimal normal subgroup of a finite characteristically simple group, collect its distinct automorphic images, use characteristic simplicity to show they generate the whole group, and use pairwise commuting minimal normals to obtain an internal direct product of isomorphic simple factors.

items.title: The socle is characteristic and decomposes as a direct product of minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Automorphisms permute the minimal normal subgroups, so the subgroup they generate is characteristic. A maximal irredundant family of minimal normal subgroups then centralizes pairwise, and the direct-product theorem shows their product is the whole socle.

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups of faithful primitive groups are transitive
items.strategy: Apply the published primitive-action normal-subgroup theorem to a minimal normal subgroup. Faithfulness rules out containment in the kernel, so the subgroup must be transitive.

items.title: Two distinct minimal normal subgroups of a primitive group are regular
items.strategy: Distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize one another and are transitive. If one element of one subgroup fixes a point, transitivity of the other and commutation force it to fix every point, so faithfulness makes it trivial.

items.title: A finite primitive group has at most two minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Any two distinct minimal normal subgroups are regular. A third one would centralize one of them and hence act regularly too, forcing two distinct point stabilizers inside a regular group, which is impossible.

items.title: A unique abelian minimal normal subgroup gives affine type
items.strategy: An abelian minimal normal subgroup in a faithful primitive group is regular. Minimality plus finite abelian-group structure makes it elementary abelian, and the conjugation action of a point stabilizer on this vector space is faithful with no nontrivial invariant subspace.

items.title: Almost simple finite groups
Affine, almost simple, diagonal, product action, and twisted wreath types
Product-action wreath products are primitive under the standard hypotheses
items.strategy: Work with the standard product action of H wr K on Delta^ell. Primitivity of H together with transitivity of K lets one push any nontrivial block across coordinates until it contains a whole fibre, and the hypotheses then force the block to be singleton or all of Delta^ell.

items.title: This page uses the coarse five-type O'Nan-Scott convention
The O'Nan-Scott classification of finite primitive groups
items.strategy: Record the sourced five-type classification in the page's fixed convention map. The local socle lemmas explain the type language, but the classification itself is kept as a bounded survey theorem rather than a new dependency spine.

items.title: CFSG enters later refinements of the O'Nan-Scott reduction
Finite 2-transitive groups have affine or almost simple socle type
items.strategy: Combine the O'Nan-Scott landscape with the extra restriction imposed by two-transitivity. Diagonal, product-action, and twisted-wreath types fail the sourced finite 2-transitivity constraints, leaving only the affine and almost simple cases.

items.title: The O'Nan-Scott theorem reduces finite primitive-group questions to socle types
FALSE: the socle is always a single simple group
items.strategy: Refute with a finite characteristically simple minimal normal subgroup that is a direct product of several isomorphic simple factors, or with a primitive group of product or diagonal type.

items.title: FALSE: every primitive group has a unique minimal normal subgroup
items.strategy: Refute with the primitive groups that have two distinct regular minimal normal subgroups, exactly the exceptional case isolated by the socle analysis.

items.title: FALSE: the O'Nan-Scott theorem is the classification of finite simple groups
items.strategy: The O'Nan-Scott theorem classifies finite primitive permutation actions by socle type. CFSG classifies finite simple groups themselves, and the two theorems serve different purposes.

items.title: FALSE: the O'Nan-Scott theorem requires the classification of finite simple groups
items.strategy: The structural classification of primitive groups by type precedes the CFSG-dependent refinements. What later uses CFSG is the detailed analysis of the almost simple and related families.

title: Socles and the Onan Scott Landscape — Examples

items.title: The natural action of AGL(1,p) is affine type
items.strategy: Identify the translation subgroup of AGL(1,p) with the unique regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup and the multiplicative subgroup with the point stabilizer acting irreducibly on it.

items.title: The natural action of A_n is almost simple type
items.strategy: For n at least 5, the socle of S_n or A_n in the natural primitive action is A_n itself, a nonabelian simple group sitting between its inner and full automorphism groups.

items.title: A simple diagonal action
items.strategy: Use T times T acting on the cosets of the diagonal subgroup of T times T. The socle has two simple factors and the diagonal subgroup identifies the standard diagonal type.

items.title: A primitive product-action wreath product
items.strategy: Take a primitive group H on Delta and a transitive group K on ell coordinates, and examine the induced action of H wr K on Delta^ell. The coordinate action displays the product-action type exactly.

items.title: A primitive group with two regular minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Use a diagonal-type or holomorph-style primitive action in which left and right regular copies of the socle centralize one another and both act regularly.

items.title: The socle of a finite solvable primitive group is elementary abelian and regular
items.strategy: A minimal normal subgroup of a finite solvable group contains a nontrivial abelian normal subgroup and hence is abelian. The affine-type proposition then forces the socle to be the unique regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup.

items.title: A transitive imprimitive action can have a nontransitive minimal normal subgroup
items.strategy: Use an imprimitive wreath-product action where a base-group factor is normal but supported on one block. The action is transitive, but that minimal normal subgroup is not.

items.title: Geodesic segments, geodesic triangles, and geodesic metric spaces
Delta-slim triangles and hyperbolic spaces
Cayley trees are 0-hyperbolic
items.strategy: In a tree each pair of vertices is joined by a unique geodesic, so the three sides of a geodesic triangle meet in a tripod. Every point of one side then lies on one of the other two sides, giving 0-slimness.

items.title: The Gromov product based at a point
Slim triangles, the Gromov product, and the four-point condition are equivalent up to constants
items.strategy: Translate slimness into lower bounds for the Gromov product, compare the three branch lengths in a geodesic triangle, and then rewrite those inequalities into the four-point form. Each implication changes constants explicitly rather than pretending one universal delta survives every reformulation.

items.title: Hyperbolic spaces have thin geodesic quadrilaterals
items.strategy: Cut a geodesic quadrilateral into two triangles along a diagonal and apply slimness to each triangle. The union of the two resulting neighbourhood bounds gives a thin-quadrilateral constant depending only on delta.

items.title: Morse stability of quasi-geodesics
items.strategy: Project a quasi-geodesic to a geodesic with the same endpoints, use thin quadrilaterals to control successive projection jumps, and bootstrap the local control to a global Hausdorff-distance bound depending on delta and the quasi-geodesic constants.

items.title: Hyperbolicity is a quasi-isometry invariant of geodesic spaces
items.strategy: Send geodesic triangles across a quasi-isometry. Their images are quasi-geodesic triangles, Morse stability compares them with honest geodesics, and the four-point or slim-triangle characterisation then transfers hyperbolicity back to the target space.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups
Hyperbolicity of a finitely generated group is independent of the finite generating set
items.strategy: Different finite generating sets give bilipschitz equivalent word metrics and hence quasi-isometric Cayley graphs. Hyperbolicity is therefore unchanged by replacing the generating set.

items.title: Finite groups and free groups are hyperbolic
items.strategy: Finite Cayley graphs have bounded diameter, so every geodesic triangle is diameter-slim. Free groups are hyperbolic because their Cayley graphs are trees, hence 0-hyperbolic.

items.title: Free abelian groups of rank at least two are not hyperbolic
items.strategy: In the standard Cayley graph of Z^2 one finds geodesic rectangles of arbitrarily large width. A fixed slimness constant would force every long side to stay uniformly close to the other two sides, which fails for the midpoints of these rectangles.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups admit finite Dehn presentations
items.strategy: Choose a finite generating set and use the hyperbolic geometry of geodesic bigons and triangles to produce relators with a uniform Dehn-shortening property. The result is stated in the exact finite-presentation form needed for the word-problem corollary.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups have solvable word problem
items.strategy: Run the Dehn reduction procedure attached to the Dehn presentation from the previous theorem. Strict length decrease gives termination, and the Dehn property gives correctness.

items.title: Linear isoperimetric characterisation of hyperbolic groups
items.strategy: Use hyperbolicity to control the area of van Kampen fillings linearly in boundary length, and conversely build slimness from a linear filling inequality by analysing geodesic polygons in the Cayley 2-complex. The area convention is fixed explicitly so the constants are meaningful.

items.title: Finite C'(1/6) presentations define hyperbolic groups
items.strategy: Use the sourced small-cancellation Dehn and linear-isoperimetric consequences to bridge finite C'(1/6) presentations to hyperbolicity. This item is kept as a survey-level agreement theorem and is not allowed to carry later dependencies until GT-8 is on disk.

items.title: Infinite-order elements of hyperbolic groups are undistorted
items.strategy: Powers of an infinite-order element define a uniform quasi-geodesic in the Cayley graph. Morse stability then compares this orbit line with a geodesic axis and yields linear growth of word length in the exponent.

items.title: The centralizer of an infinite-order element in a hyperbolic group is virtually cyclic
items.strategy: Every centralizing element preserves the quasi-axis of the given infinite-order element up to bounded distance. The induced action on the axis gives a homomorphism to the isometry group of a quasi-line with finite kernel, forcing a finite-index cyclic subgroup.

items.title: Abelian subgroups of hyperbolic groups are virtually cyclic
items.strategy: An infinite abelian subgroup contains an infinite-order element, and every element of the subgroup centralizes it. The subgroup therefore lies in a virtually cyclic centralizer.

items.title: Finite subgroups of a hyperbolic group have uniformly bounded order
items.strategy: A finite subgroup orbit has bounded diameter, so one may choose a point minimizing maximal displacement and then compare the finite subgroup action with the uniformly locally finite geometry of the Cayley graph. Hyperbolicity bounds the possible displacement patterns and hence the subgroup order.

items.title: Elementary and non-elementary hyperbolic groups
Non-elementary hyperbolic groups contain a rank-two free subgroup
items.strategy: Choose two independent infinite-order elements with sufficiently separated quasi-axes and apply ping-pong on large translates of their attracting regions. The resulting subgroup is free of rank two.

items.title: The Gromov boundary via asymptotic sequences
Asymptoticity of Gromov sequences is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate from the definition. Transitivity uses the Gromov-product inequality coming from hyperbolicity to keep pairwise products uniformly large after passing through an intermediate sequence.

items.title: The boundary topology defined by Gromov products
The boundary topology is well defined and quasi-isometry invariant
items.strategy: Compare boundary neighbourhoods defined using different basepoints and different representative sequences by the four-point inequalities. A quasi-isometry sends divergent quasi-geodesic rays to divergent quasi-geodesic rays, so Morse stability induces the boundary homeomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: a hyperbolic group is just a group with a hyperbolic-plane subgroup
items.strategy: Finite groups and free groups are hyperbolic, but neither notion is defined by containing a copy of the hyperbolic plane. Hyperbolicity is a Cayley-graph property, not a subgroup test of that form.

items.title: FALSE: the same delta works after every finite change of generating set
items.strategy: Hyperbolicity is invariant under quasi-isometry, but the proof changes constants. Bilipschitz equivalent word metrics need not preserve one universal slimness constant.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian group is hyperbolic
items.strategy: The group Z^2 is finitely generated abelian but not hyperbolic, as witnessed by arbitrarily large geodesic rectangles in its Cayley graph.

items.title: FALSE: all quasi-geodesics in all metric spaces stay uniformly close to geodesics
items.strategy: Morse stability is a hyperbolic-space theorem. Euclidean planes already contain quasi-geodesics that drift arbitrarily far from every geodesic with the same endpoints.

items.title: FALSE: the Gromov boundary definition needs no properness or equivalence check
items.strategy: The boundary construction here depends on asymptoticity being an equivalence relation and on the proper geodesic hypotheses that make the topology behave as stated. Dropping those hypotheses changes the object.

title: Hyperbolic Spaces and Hyperbolic Groups — Examples

items.title: Every tree is 0-hyperbolic
items.strategy: In a tree every geodesic triangle is a tripod, so each side lies in the union of the other two. This is the model zero-hyperbolic example behind free groups.

items.title: The hyperbolic plane is hyperbolic
items.strategy: Use the classical geodesic-triangle comparison in the hyperbolic plane to obtain a uniform slimness constant. The example is geometric rather than combinatorial, but it fits the same definition verbatim.

items.title: Free groups have Cantor-set boundaries
items.strategy: The Cayley graph of a free group is a regular tree, so boundary points are infinite reduced rays. Identifying rays with infinite reduced words gives the usual Cantor-set model of the boundary.

items.title: Closed surface groups are hyperbolic
items.strategy: A cocompact torsion-free lattice in the isometry group of the hyperbolic plane acts geometrically on H^2. Hyperbolicity of the plane and Svarc-Milnor then make the surface group hyperbolic.

items.title: A small-cancellation presentation gives a hyperbolic group
items.strategy: Choose a finite presentation satisfying the strict C'(1/6) overlap condition and apply the sourced agreement theorem. The example is a concrete witness that small cancellation lands inside the hyperbolic world.

items.title: Z^2 is not hyperbolic
items.strategy: Work in the standard square-grid Cayley graph. Midpoints of long sides of geodesic squares move arbitrarily far from the other two sides, so no uniform slimness constant exists.

items.title: A product of two infinite groups need not be hyperbolic
items.strategy: The direct product Z times Z is the simplest witness. It is infinite in both factors and fails hyperbolicity for the same large-rectangle reason as the free abelian rank-two case.
